doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Recording old Hollywood string and brass players
summary: He worked with veteran Hollywood and New York string and brass players, using a standard 12-4-4-2 string section and a date of 65 pieces.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Yup. In New York and LA. And I was lucky enough to come along when there were still a lot of those guys around, the brass, woodwinds, and the string players. They were old Hollywood guys. They played on the movies going back into the late 40s and 50s. And they were phenomenal. You had a concert master and it was for real. And we usually cut our strings 12-4-4-2; 12 violins, 4 violi, 4 celli, 2 double basses, upright basses. And I would have to pay them but once we got that it was really quick with the charts. The main thing was to run it down and correct mistakes in the chart. He’d circle things up on the stand with the conductor and then the copyists would be there, the arranger and they would “on bar 64 change the e to an e flat” for each, if there was a mistake in the charts or something didn’t fit right. But then it was always first or second take. And then I would double the strings and sometimes triple them. But we wouldn’t just triple them with the same, we’d move the mics a little bit. They were all miced up there like this. Some were close miced. But if there was a little step out with a violin or something we’d close mic that but everything else was overheads. Like a classical orchestra. And you had to get it quick with that many people in the studio. If you had a 12-4-4 and 2 string section, but then if you were adding brass I mean I think the largest section I ever did was maybe 65 pieces at once, including live drums and live bass and live guitar and live piano.
